---
title: "More info"
---

<div class="intro-text">
<p>This is the <strong>MVP prediction machine</strong> — below are two different ways of ranking who's having the best MVP case this season.</p>

<p>The first table uses my own <strong>custom MVP score</strong>, a weighted formula I built by hand that combines stats like points per game, assists per game, rebounds per game, team win percentage, and more. I chose the weights myself based on what I think matters most for an MVP case.</p>

<p>The second table uses a <strong>trained machine learning model</strong> instead. I trained a logistic regression model on 10 seasons of past MVP winners, so instead of me picking the weights, the model learned on its own which stats actually tend to separate MVP winners from everyone else. It then estimates each current player's probability of winning MVP this season based on those learned patterns.</p>

<p>You may wonder what the pros and cons of logistic regression are in this context. <b><i>The main advantage</b></i> is that it outputs probabilities, which can be sorted directly into a ranking, and it is simple enough to avoid overfitting when there are only about 10 MVP seasons to learn from. <b><i>The main drawbacks </b></i> are that it assumes a linear relationship between stats and MVP likelihood, so it can miss nonlinear effects, and it relies on stats alone, so it ignores factors like narrative and voter fatigue. Class weighting also inflates the probabilities, so they are best used for ranking rather than as literal chances of winning. Another drawback is that most players have very low, nearly identical MVP probabilities, so the model is only really useful for separating the top contenders. Differences among the rest are small and should not be over-interpreted. If you wonder for why are there only about 10 seasons, well that is due to the fact of the modern NBA era where players have drastically changed as the game itself has evolved, as the data itself was from the 2016 season onwards.    </p>

<p>Because of these limits, the model likely misses several things that influence real MVP voting:</p>
<ul>
  <li><strong>Narrative and voter psychology:</strong> storylines, "his turn" voting, and voter fatigue are not captured by box-score stats.</li>
  <li><strong>Injuries and games played:</strong> a player with big per-game numbers who missed many games can still score well here, even though voters penalize availability.</li>
  <li><strong>Defense:</strong> blocks and steals capture only a small part of a player's defensive impact.</li>
  <li><strong>Era differences:</strong> scoring and pace change over time, so the same stat line can mean different things in different seasons.</li>
  <li><strong>Competition within a season:</strong> MVP is a relative choice among players, but the model scores each player-season on its own.</li>
  <li><strong>Clutch play and playoff reputation:</strong> these shape how voters view a player but are not in the data.</li>
</ul>

<p class="intro-highlight">Comparing the two is part of the fun — sometimes they agree, sometimes they don't, and the players ranked below are whoever came out on top in each method this season. There are also graphs further down showing how individual stats relate to MVP outcomes.</p>

<p><i>If you want to modify the calculator yourself and set your own formula to determine the MVP winner, you are also able to do that.</i></p>
</div>
